title: 1 Samuel 18:17–30
context: Saul offers his elder daughter Merab if David will fight the LORD’s battles, secretly hoping the Philistines will kill him; then Merab is given to another man. When Saul learns that his daughter Michal loves David, he offers her for a bride-price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, again hoping David will fall. David brings two hundred and marries Michal. Saul sees that the LORD is with David, grows more afraid and becomes David’s enemy continually, while David’s name grows highly esteemed. The Masoretic Text has two hundred in verse 27, while the Septuagint reads one hundred, matching the number David later cites in 2 Samuel 3:14. In that shorter form, often listed from Codex Vaticanus, 18:17–19 and 18:29b–30 are among the verses absent. Both traditions read the section as showing that Saul’s schemes cannot overturn what God is doing for David, while Saul remains accountable for them.

verses.text: Saul said to David, “Behold, my elder daughter Merab. I will give her to you as wife. Only be valiant for me, and fight the LORD’s battles.” For Saul said, “Don’t let my hand be on him, but let the hand of the Philistines be on him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul offers David his elder daughter Merab if David will be valiant and fight the LORD’s battles, while privately hoping the Philistines will kill him. Saul’s offer is a trap.

Arminian readers note that Saul uses pious language to cover murderous intent, a sobering warning that religious words can mask sinful purposes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s calculation to let the Philistines do what he will not do himself shows a hardened heart, and that God will frustrate the scheme by preserving David through the very battles meant to destroy him.

Both traditions see Saul’s deception as narrative exposing his guilt and God’s protection of David.

verses.text: David said to Saul, “Who am I, and what is my life, or my father’s family in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks who he is, and what his life or his father’s family is in Israel, that he should be the king’s son-in-law. David responds with humility.

Arminian readers note that David’s modesty appears genuine and that he does not grasp at honor, choosing humility even when advancement is offered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s question echoes the humility of others God raised up, such as Gideon (Judges 6:15), and that God exalts those who do not exalt themselves. It may also reflect the custom of a modest reply to a royal offer.

Both traditions honor David’s humility while noting that the offer itself was made in bad faith.

verses.text: But at the time when Merab, Saul’s daughter, should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite as wife.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the time comes for Merab to be given to David, she is given instead to Adriel the Meholathite. Saul breaks his promise.

Arminian readers note that Saul’s broken promise shows his untrustworthiness, and that David must endure injustice without retaliating, which he does.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s unfaithfulness contrasts with God’s faithfulness to his promises, and that God will give David a wife and a kingdom in his own time. At 2 Samuel 21:8 some manuscripts read Merab where the Masoretic Text reads Michal.

Both traditions see the broken promise as part of the narrative of Saul’s decline and David’s patient endurance.

verses.text: Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved David; and they told Saul, and the thing pleased him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Michal, Saul’s daughter, loves David, and when Saul is told, the news pleases him. Saul sees an opportunity.

Arminian readers note that Michal’s love is sincere, while Saul’s pleasure is calculated; the contrast shows how one person’s sincere affection can be exploited by another’s selfish purposes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Michal is often noted as the only woman in Old Testament narrative explicitly said to love a man, and that her love becomes part of the providential story in which God protects David (19:11–17).

Both traditions read Michal’s love as real and Saul’s response as manipulative.

verses.text: Saul said, I will give her to him, that she may be a snare to him and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him. Therefore Saul said to David a second time, “You shall today be my son-in-law.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul thinks he will give Michal to David so that she may be a snare to him and the Philistines may kill him, and he tells David a second time that he will be his son-in-law. Saul plans to use his daughter as bait.

Arminian readers note that Saul’s willingness to use his own daughter shows how far envy has corrupted him, and that sin progressively distorts relationships.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s scheme ironically sets in place the very circumstances God will use to protect David, since Michal will later save his life (19:11–17).

Both traditions see God overruling Saul’s evil intentions for good.

verses.text: Saul commanded his servants, “Talk with David secretly, and say, ‘Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you. Now therefore be the king’s son-in-law.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul commands his servants to speak to David secretly, telling him the king delights in him and all his servants love him, and urging him to become the king’s son-in-law. Saul uses flattery.

Arminian readers note that the deceptive message contains truth, since the people do love David, but Saul twists it to manipulate him, a warning about how truth can be misused.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul works through intermediaries to conceal his intent, yet God sees what is hidden, and the plot will fail despite its secrecy.

Both traditions read Saul’s flattery as narrative of deception that cannot ultimately prevail against God’s purposes for David.

verses.text: Saul’s servants spoke those words in the ears of David. David said, “Does it seem to you a light thing to be the king’s son-in-law, since I am a poor man and little known?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul’s servants speak these words to David, who asks whether it seems a light thing to be the king’s son-in-law, since he is poor and little known. David raises the question of the bride-price.

Arminian readers note that David’s humility again appears, and that he is honest about his limits rather than pretending to wealth or status he does not have.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s poverty is part of the pattern by which God raises the lowly to high places (2:8), so that David’s rise cannot be attributed to wealth or connections.

Both traditions see David’s honest humility as a mark of his character.

verses.text: The servants of Saul told him, saying, “David spoke like this.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul’s servants report David’s words to him. The conversation is relayed back to the king.

Arminian readers note that the exchange through messengers shows Saul carefully managing the situation to achieve his ends, and that he responds to David’s humility not with compassion but with further scheming.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that every report and response in this chain is under God’s oversight, so that Saul’s calculated maneuvering serves God’s purpose of bringing David closer to the throne.

Both traditions read the verse as part of the narrative’s careful build-up toward the bride-price Saul is about to set.

verses.text: Saul said, “Tell David, ‘The king desires no dowry except one hundred foreskins of the Philistines, to be avenged of the king’s enemies.’ ” Now Saul thought he would make David fall by the hand of the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul sets the bride-price as no dowry except a hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on the king’s enemies, intending that David fall by the Philistines. Saul’s real motive is stated plainly.

Arminian readers note that Saul’s demand appears patriotic but is designed to kill David, a striking example of how sinful intent can hide behind public duty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator exposes Saul’s hidden purpose so that the reader sees God’s protection all the more clearly when David survives and returns triumphant.

Both traditions read the bride-price as narrative of Saul’s treachery, without commending the practice itself.

verses.text: When his servants told David these words, it pleased David well to be the king’s son-in-law. Before the deadline,
verses.arminianNotes:
When the servants tell David, it pleases him to become the king’s son-in-law, and before the deadline expires he prepares to act. David accepts the challenge.

Arminian readers note that David willingly takes on the dangerous task, trusting God’s protection while acting with energy and purpose rather than waiting passively.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s acceptance moves him further into the role God has prepared, and that the danger Saul intended becomes another occasion for God’s faithfulness to be shown.

Both traditions see David’s response as courageous, while recognizing that the narrative does not present the bride-price as a model to imitate.

verses.text: David arose and went, he and his men, and killed two hundred men of the Philistines. Then David brought their foreskins, and they gave them in full number to the king, that he might be the king’s son-in-law. Then Saul gave him Michal his daughter as wife.
verses.arminianNotes:
David and his men go out, kill two hundred Philistines, and bring their foreskins in full number to the king, and Saul gives him Michal as wife. The Septuagint reads one hundred, matching 2 Samuel 3:14.

Arminian readers note that the Hebrew number shows David exceeding the demand, while the textual difference is real and need not be resolved with certainty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s plan fails completely: David survives, fulfills the demand, and becomes the king’s son-in-law, a clear sign that God’s hand is on him. Scholars weigh whether the Hebrew or Greek number is older.

Both traditions read the outcome as God’s protection of David and as narrative rather than prescription.

verses.text: Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David; and Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul sees and knows that the LORD is with David, and that Michal loves him. Saul cannot deny the truth.

Arminian readers note that Saul’s recognition of God’s presence with David leaves him without excuse, and that his continuing hostility is a chosen resistance to what he clearly perceives.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the verse sums up the chapter’s theme: the LORD is with David, and even David’s enemy perceives it, which underlines that God’s purposes are unmistakable even to those who oppose them.

Both traditions see Saul’s knowledge as deepening his responsibility.

verses.text: Saul was even more afraid of David; and Saul was David’s enemy continually.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul becomes even more afraid of David, and Saul is David’s enemy continually. The hostility becomes permanent.

Arminian readers note that Saul’s repeated choices to resist God’s purpose lead to a settled enmity, illustrating how unrepented sin can harden into a lasting disposition.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s continual enmity reflects a heart that God has given over to its chosen course, while Saul remains wholly responsible for his hatred, a balance that runs through this narrative.

Both traditions see the verse as marking the settled opposition that will drive the following chapters.

verses.text: Then the princes of the Philistines went out; and as often as they went out, David behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was highly esteemed.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistine princes go out to battle, and each time David acts more wisely than all of Saul’s servants, so that his name becomes highly esteemed. The chapter closes with David’s honor.

Arminian readers note that David’s consistent wise conduct earns him a good name, and that faithfulness over time builds a reputation God can use.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God exalts David’s name, anticipating the promise of a great name in 2 Samuel 7:9, and that David’s rise is ultimately God’s doing, even when it comes through his own skill in battle.

Both traditions close the chapter honoring God’s faithfulness to David and David’s faithful service.
